lessons.title: The quarterback
lessons.objective: You can say why everyone talks about the quarterback.

payload.prompt: Why is the quarterback the most talked-about player on a team?

options.text: He runs the offense and decides where the ball goes on every play
He wears number one
He is the tallest player on the team

explanation.correct: The quarterback controls the offense. He takes the snap, reads the defense, and throws or hands off. Every big play depends on him.
explanation.incorrect: The quarterback is the decision-maker on offense. He chooses where to throw or run the ball, making him the most important player.

payload.prompt: What happens if the quarterback throws an interception in the end zone?

options.text: The other team gets the ball deep in their own territory
The quarterback's team scores a safety
The play is automatically reviewed

explanation.correct: An interception in the end zone is a turnover. The defense takes over the ball and usually has great field position to score.
explanation.incorrect: A quarterback interception turns the ball over to the defense. In the end zone it is especially bad because the other team starts deep in your own territory.

statement.speaker: Fan at game
statement.text: Our quarterback is a pocket passer. He needs time to let plays develop.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: He wears a special vest under his jersey
He throws from inside the blockers' protection, not on the move, so the offensive line must give him time
He only throws to receivers in the slot
He carries the ball in his pocket at halftime

payload.translation: A pocket passer stays in the clean area the blockers create and throws downfield. He is different from a mobile quarterback who runs around and improvises.

followUps.line: Is he fast, or just good at throwing?
followUps.why: Tests whether you understand that pocket passers succeed with accuracy and timing, not mobility.

followUps.line: Why does the line have to protect him?
followUps.why: Shows you know that rushers ending the pocket forces bad throws.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, listen for context clues. Fans talk about time to throw and how the line performs around pocket passers.

statement.speaker: Coach on TV
statement.text: The offensive coordinator called a great play that played to the quarterback's strength.

payload.question: Who is the offensive coordinator?

options.text: The head coach's assistant who designs and often calls the passing plays and offensive strategy
The quarterback's personal trainer
An official who makes sure both teams follow the rules
The guy who hands the ball to the quarterback

payload.translation: The offensive coordinator works with the head coach to design the team's offensive scheme and calls most of the plays you see. Great play-calling puts your best players in position to succeed.

followUps.line: Why would a coordinator choose one play over another?
followUps.why: Helps you understand that coaches read defenses and choose plays to exploit weaknesses.

followUps.line: Can the quarterback change the play?
followUps.why: Tests if you know about audibles, when the QB changes the play at the line.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The coordinator is part of the coaching staff, not a player. If unsure, ask what coordinators control on their side of the ball.

payload.prompt: If the starter gets injured, the backup becomes the public face of the franchise. True or false?

scene.alt: A field showing a quarterback being helped off the field by trainers while the backup warms up on the sideline.

explanation.correct: True. Once a backup starts playing full-time, he becomes the public face of the offense and the team, even if the starter returns later.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, whoever is playing the most is the face of the team. Fan focus shifts to the guy on the field.

lessons.title: Backs, receivers and tight ends
lessons.objective: You can tell the skill positions apart by what they do.

payload.prompt: Match each skill position to what they do.

pairs.definition: Lines up behind the quarterback; runs the ball, catches passes, sometimes blocks.
Lines up wide and runs routes to catch passes.
A hybrid who blocks like a lineman and catches like a receiver.

explanation.summary: Running backs are versatile, receivers are pass-catchers, and tight ends do both jobs at once.
explanation.sayThisLine: Running back runs and catches, wide receiver just catches, tight end does both and blocks.

payload.prompt: Match each skill position to their strength.

pairs.definition: Best at finding open grass, reading blocks and catching the ball in space.
Best at running precise routes, creating separation and making contested catches.
Best at gaining yards after the catch near the goal line and blocking in the run game.

explanation.summary: Each position brings different skills. Great offenses use all three well.
explanation.sayThisLine: Backs run free, receivers catch deep, tight ends block and go over the middle.

payload.prompt: Tap the wide receiver split out wide in this formation.

diagram.alt: An offensive formation showing a player split out wide from the line.

explanation.correct: Right. A wide receiver split out alone is in the receiver slot, away from the line of scrimmage.
explanation.incorrect: Look for the player spread out wide from the line. That positioning makes him the receiver.

payload.prompt: Tap the tight end lined up on the line of scrimmage.

diagram.alt: A formation showing running back depth, tight end on the line, and wide receiver split out.

explanation.correct: The tight end lines up right on the line next to the offensive line. Running backs stay back; receivers split out wide.
explanation.incorrect: Look for the player who lines up next to the big men on the line. That is the tight end.

payload.prompt: A running back catches a pass 5 yards out and runs 20 more. Why praise this play?

options.text: He had great athletic ability to run that far
He had the strength to break tackles after catching the ball
He caught the pass at exactly the right depth

explanation.correct: Running backs who turn short passes into big gains are extremely valuable. That 20 yards after the catch is what makes him dangerous.
explanation.incorrect: Yards after the catch (YAC) is the mark of an elite receiver or back. Breaking tackles after catching is what turns a nothing play into a touchdown run.

lessons.title: The big guys up front
lessons.objective: You can explain what the offensive line is protecting and why fans love a good one.

payload.prompt: What is the offensive line's main job on a passing play?

options.text: Create a protective bubble (the pocket) so the quarterback has time to throw
Catch the ball if the quarterback is in trouble
Tell the quarterback which receiver to throw to

explanation.correct: The offensive line (five big men) blocks the defensive rushers to give the quarterback time in the pocket to find open receivers.
explanation.incorrect: The offensive line protects the quarterback from pass rushers. A good line gives him time; a bad one makes him scramble.

payload.prompt: Why do running backs look for holes created by the offensive line?

options.text: The holes are gaps the line creates by moving defenders out of the way
The holes are where the ball was just buried
Holes are pretend, running backs just run straight

explanation.correct: On running plays, the offensive line blocks defenders and opens gaps (holes) for the back to run through. The best backs read the blocks and hit the right hole.
explanation.incorrect: Run blocking is all about creating openings. The line has to move their guys off the spot so the back gets through.

payload.prompt: Tap the five offensive linemen in this formation.

diagram.alt: A football field showing 11 offensive players lined up with the five big linemen clearly positioned on the line of scrimmage.

explanation.correct: The five linemen form a wall: center in the middle snaps the ball, guards next to the center, and tackles on the ends. They work together to protect the quarterback and open holes.
explanation.incorrect: The five offensive linemen are the big guys on the line: center, two guards, two tackles. They are the foundation of the offense.

payload.prompt: Tap the defensive linemen trying to rush through the offensive line.

diagram.alt: A football field showing offense on one side and defense across from them at the line of scrimmage, with defensive linemen poised to rush.

explanation.correct: The defensive line is the first group trying to rush past the offensive line to get to the quarterback or running back. Usually three or four defenders.
explanation.incorrect: Look for the big defenders lined up across from the offensive line. They rush first on passing plays.

payload.prompt: A great offensive line can single-handedly win games. True or false?

scene.alt: An offensive line standing tall in formation, creating a clear pocket while blocking effectively.

explanation.correct: True. A great offensive line gives the quarterback time to throw and opens holes for the running game. Both can decide games.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, a dominant line can control the game. Bad lines lose games no matter how talented the skill players are.

lessons.title: Linebackers and defensive backs
lessons.objective: You can name the defenders behind the line and what each one covers.

payload.prompt: Match each defensive position to their role.

pairs.definition: Defenders behind the line who stop runs, rush the passer and cover backs and tight ends.
A defensive back who lines up wide and covers receivers.
The deepest defenders, the last line against big plays. Free safety and strong safety.

explanation.summary: Linebackers are the middle of the defense, corners cover the sidelines, and safeties are the last resort deep.
explanation.sayThisLine: Linebacker reads the play, corner covers the receiver, safety is your backup if he beats the corner.

payload.prompt: Match each position to where they typically line up.

pairs.definition: About 3-5 yards behind the line of scrimmage, in the middle of the field.
7-10 yards off the line, out wide covering the receiver.
10-15 yards back, deep in the middle or split to the sides, protecting the end zone.

explanation.summary: The closer to the line, the better for stopping runs. The deeper you are, the better for stopping the deep pass.
explanation.sayThisLine: Linebackers are tight to stop the run, corners match the receivers, safeties roam the deep field.

payload.prompt: Identify the linebacker, cornerback and safety in this defensive formation.

diagram.alt: A defensive formation showing defensive linemen on the line, linebackers behind them, cornerbacks out wide, and safeties deep.

explanation.correct: The linebacker reads the play from behind the line, the corners cover the receivers wide, and the safeties play deep as the last help.
explanation.incorrect: Look for defenders lined up at different depths: linebackers close to the line, corners out wide, safeties deep.

payload.prompt: If a receiver runs a route, which defenders are responsible for covering him?

diagram.alt: A field showing an offensive receiver running a route downfield with defensive backs in position to cover.

explanation.correct: The cornerback stays tight on the receiver, and the safety plays deep to help if the receiver beats the corner or the route goes over the top.
explanation.incorrect: On a pass route, the corner covers the receiver and the safety provides help deep over the top.

payload.prompt: A great linebacker reads run vs pass from the first step. True or false?

scene.alt: A defensive formation with a linebacker watching the running back's first movement at the snap.

explanation.correct: True. A great linebacker reads the backfield instantly. Run or pass, pass-rush or drop back—the first step tells him.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, a smart linebacker can read the play at the snap. That is what makes elite defenders so valuable.

lessons.title: What she means by the secondary
lessons.objective: You can decode a sentence about the secondary.

statement.speaker: Fan complaining
statement.text: Our secondary is getting torched today. The quarterback has all day to throw.

payload.question: What is the secondary failing at?

options.text: Protecting the quarterback in the pocket
Covering receivers and preventing big pass plays
Stopping the running game
Calling timeouts to regroup

payload.translation: The secondary is the defensive backs (corners and safeties). If they are getting torched, receivers are beating them and the quarterback has open targets downfield.

followUps.line: Is it the corners or the safeties playing badly?
followUps.why: Shows you can distinguish which part of the secondary failed.

followUps.line: Do they need more help from the linebackers?
followUps.why: Tests if you understand coverage schemes and help from other positions.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, notice the fan said the quarterback has time. That means the pass rush is not the problem; the coverage is.

statement.speaker: Analyst on TV
statement.text: The strong safety is cheating up. If that quarterback hits the skinny post, it is six.

payload.question: What does cheating up mean?

options.text: The safety is standing closer to the line of scrimmage than usual, helping against the run but risking big passes over his head
The safety secretly watched film on the opponent
The safety gets an extra timeout
The referee is helping the defense

payload.translation: Safety alignment reveals strategy. Cheating up means they expect a run or short pass. A post route down the seam creates a mismatch because the safety is too close.

followUps.line: Why would the coach tell the safety to cheat up?
followUps.why: Tests if you understand the run-pass read and scheme adjustments.
Shows you know that safety coverage has trade-offs.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Cheating up means adjusting position, not actual rule-breaking. Think about how safeties position themselves based on down and distance.

payload.prompt: What is the secondary's most important job?

options.text: Tackle the running back in the backfield
Cover receivers and prevent them from catching passes
Tackle the quarterback before he throws

explanation.correct: The secondary covers pass routes. Corners guard receivers, safeties cover the deep field. A secondary that covers well forces bad decisions.
explanation.incorrect: The secondary (defensive backs) is built to cover receivers. When coverage breaks down, big plays happen.

payload.prompt: What is the difference between a cornerback and a strong safety?

options.text: Corners line up wide covering receivers one-on-one; safeties line up deep and help cover the middle
There is no difference; they do the same job
Safeties only cover backs and tight ends; corners only cover receivers

explanation.correct: Cornerbacks match up with receivers at the line. Safeties (free and strong) play deep and help over the top. The strong safety also helps against the run.
explanation.incorrect: Corners are assigned to receivers and play the sideline. Safeties roam the deep field and support run defense.

payload.prompt: Match each secondary position to what they excel at.

pairs.definition: Excellent at tight coverage on receivers, press coverage and closing on the ball in the air.
Deep help over the top, reading the quarterback and helping corners when receivers beat them.
Close support against the run and shorter passing routes, often lined up over the tight end.

explanation.summary: Great secondaries mix specialized roles. Corners press receivers, free safeties help deep, strong safeties help near the line.
explanation.sayThisLine: Corner plays the receiver, free safety is over the top, strong safety is in the middle.

lessons.title: Reading a jersey
lessons.objective: You can guess a player's position from his number.

payload.prompt: Tap the player most likely to be the quarterback by jersey number.

diagram.alt: Five football players in uniform showing different jersey numbers: 7, 42, 63, 89, and 15.

explanation.correct: Quarterbacks wear 1-19. Number 7 is in that range. It is a strong signal for the position.
explanation.incorrect: Look at the jersey numbers. Quarterbacks wear 1-19, so the lower numbers signal QB, not linemen or receivers.

payload.prompt: Tap the player most likely to be a lineman by jersey number.

diagram.alt: Three football players showing jersey numbers 19, 76, and 34.

explanation.correct: Linemen wear 50-79. Player 76 fits perfectly. Numbers are shorthand to spot positions instantly.
explanation.incorrect: Look at the number ranges. Linemen wear 50-79, so the higher numbers signal offensive or defensive line.

payload.prompt: Fill in the typical jersey number ranges for each position group.
payload.template: Quarterbacks wear {{qb-range}}, receivers and tight ends wear {{skill-range}}, and linebackers wear {{lb-range}}.

explanation.correct: QBs are 1-19, receivers/TEs are 80-89, linebackers are 40-49. These ranges help fans and officials spot eligible receivers.
explanation.incorrect: Jersey number ranges are part of the rules. Quarterbacks 1-19, skill players 1-19 and 80-89, linebackers 40-59, linemen 50-79.

payload.prompt: Fill in the eligible receiver rule.
payload.template: An eligible receiver is a player whose {{status}} and {{number}} allow him to catch a forward pass. Linemen are {{ineligible}} unless they report as eligible to the referee.

explanation.correct: The offense must line up the right players (backs, receivers, tight ends) for them to be eligible. Linemen can report as eligible but usually are not.
explanation.incorrect: Eligible receivers are determined by position and number. Linemen in the 50-79 range need to report as eligible or they cannot catch.

payload.prompt: You see a player wearing number 68 line up as a receiver wide out. What does that tell you?

options.text: He is a lineman in the 50-79 range, so that alignment is unusual and probably means he reported as eligible
He is definitely a receiver because his number is in the 80s
He is not allowed to catch passes

explanation.correct: Player 68 is a lineman (50-79 range) split out wide. That is rare and means the offense told the referee he is eligible to catch the ball on this play.
explanation.incorrect: A lineman in the 50-79 range split out wide is an eligible lineman—reported to the refs before the snap to catch on this play.

lessons.title: Coaches and depth charts
lessons.objective: You can tell a coordinator from a head coach and read a depth chart.

payload.prompt: Match each coaching role to what they do.

pairs.definition: Runs the entire team, makes final decisions on strategy, game planning and personnel.
Designs the offensive scheme and calls most of the plays during the game.
Designs the defensive scheme, calls adjustments and often signals plays from the sideline.

explanation.summary: The head coach oversees everything. The coordinators specialize and run their side of the ball.
explanation.sayThisLine: Head coach leads the team, OC builds the offense, DC builds the defense.

payload.prompt: Match these coaching roles to their responsibilities.

pairs.definition: Oversees passes, runs, formations and personnel decisions on offense.
Handles kickoffs, punts, field goals and returns—the third phase of the game.
Works one-on-one with the quarterback on mechanics, decision-making and play-calling.

explanation.summary: Each coach specializes. The OC runs the broad strategy; the QBs coach develops the quarterback.
explanation.sayThisLine: Coordinators build schemes; position coaches develop players.

payload.prompt: What does it mean if a player is listed second on the depth chart at his position?

options.text: He is the backup; the starter ahead of him starts most plays
He is injured and will not play
He plays only on special teams

explanation.correct: The depth chart ranks players at each position. First string is the starter, second string is the backup. Higher on the chart means more likely to play.
explanation.incorrect: Depth charts show the pecking order. Second means you are behind the starter and get in if he is hurt or rested.

payload.prompt: A receivers coach develops techniques for catching and running routes. What coach calls the plays?

options.text: The receivers coach designs every route
The offensive coordinator, who works with position coaches to design plays
The head coach tells the quarterback what to do every play

explanation.correct: Position coaches develop players. The offensive coordinator designs the scheme and calls plays during the game. The head coach oversees all.
explanation.incorrect: The offensive coordinator calls plays. Position coaches develop their players. The head coach sets strategy.

payload.prompt: If a team trades for a star, he automatically starts ahead in the depth chart. True or false?

scene.alt: A depth chart being updated with a new player's name added at the top of the list.

explanation.correct: True. When you trade for a proven star, he immediately replaces the incumbent starter. The depth chart reflects the coaches' judgment.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, trading for a star player means the team believes he is better than what they have. He is listed first on the depth chart.
